title: When the Confession Sings
premise: Rosalind Underhill, a retired detective turned failing bookseller, receives a confession letter for the murder of local magnate Edmund Vane — postmarked the day after his funeral, naming Rosalind as its intended recipient. The letter's details match no public record, meaning it was written by someone with access to the sealed case file, and it confesses to a crime that hasn't happened yet: the death of Edmund's heir, Cressida. As Rosalind races to protect Cressida before the reading of the will triggers the killer's endgame, they discover the confession is itself an inheritance — a poisoned legacy passed down through three generations of the Vane family, each keeper of the letter complicit in silence. In the end, Rosalind traps the killer by staging a false trial transcript, forcing a confession that sings on record, but only at the cost of exposing their own buried failure in the original Vane case.
about_author: Marguerite Eriksen is a former court stenographer from the Yorkshire coast who spent twenty years transcribing confessions she was never allowed to comment on. 'When the Confession Sings' is her third novel, drawing on her fascination with what people say when they believe no one is keeping score.

chapters.title: Postmarked Yesterday
chapters.summary: Rosalind Underhill, closing the bookshop early over unpaid rent notices, finds a thick envelope among the day's post: a full confession to the murder of Edmund Vane, postmarked the day after his funeral. The prose is elegant, unhurried, and addressed to Rosalind by their old rank. POV: Rosalind. Beat: dread wrapped in curiosity — the hook that won't let go.

chapters.title: The Case File Nobody Closed
chapters.summary: Rosalind digs out their memory of the Vane investigation from fifteen years ago, which they worked as a junior detective before leaving the force. The confession cites details never made public — the wrong-shaped wound, the moved decanter. Someone had access to the sealed file. POV: Rosalind. Beat: professional unease curdling into personal stakes.

chapters.title: Cressida in the Doorway
chapters.summary: Edmund's estranged daughter Cressida arrives at the bookshop unannounced, having received a copy of the same letter with one line added: 'You are next.' She doesn't trust police; she trusts the one detective who once told her father no. POV: alternating Rosalind/Cressida. Beat: reluctant alliance formed between two people guarding old wounds.

chapters.title: A House That Remembers
chapters.summary: The pair visit Vane House for the funeral reception, cataloguing mourners: the lawyer Harrowgate, the housekeeper Mrs. Pell, the nephew Tobias who manages the estate accounts. Every room is curated like a museum to a man everyone hated privately. POV: Cressida. Beat: grief complicated by relief — and the first sense of being watched.

chapters.title: What the Will Withholds
chapters.summary: Harrowgate reveals the will cannot be read for thirty days due to a codicil dispute — a deliberate delay someone engineered. Whoever benefits from waiting is protected; whoever needs the inheritance now is exposed. POV: Rosalind. Beat: the mystery acquires a clock.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: A second confession arrives, this one describing a murder committed thirty years ago — Edmund's business partner, ruled accidental. The handwriting matches. The killer isn't confessing to one crime but curating a family archive of them. POV: Rosalind. Beat: vertigo; the pattern is generational, not personal.

chapters.title: Mrs. Pell's Locked Drawer
chapters.summary: Rosalind searches the servants' wing and finds Mrs. Pell burning papers, saving only a photograph of three children at Vane House — Edmund, the partner's son, and a girl no one mentions. Mrs. Pell says only: 'The house keeps its own ledger.' POV: Mrs. Pell. Beat: sympathy for the keeper of secrets.

chapters.title: Tobias Counts the Money
chapters.summary: Tobias, charming and desperate, admits the estate is insolvent beneath its polish — Edmund gambled away the inheritance years ago. The fortune everyone is circling may be fictional, which makes the murders about something else entirely. POV: Tobias. Beat: red herring deepens into genuine pathos.

chapters.title: The Detective Who Left
chapters.summary: Rosalind's former colleague DI Anselm Okafor confronts them: interfering in an active-adjacent case could cost whatever pension and reputation Rosalind has left. He also lets slip that the sealed file was checked out twice last year — once under Rosalind's own authorization code. POV: Rosalind. Beat: betrayal; the frame tightens around our hero.

chapters.title: Someone Used My Name
chapters.summary: Rosalind traces the file access to a retired records clerk who recalls a woman claiming to be Rosalind's research assistant. The description fits someone at the funeral. The killer has been rehearsing Rosalind's role for months. POV: Rosalind. Beat: paranoia — the confession letters are bait in a trap built for them.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Cressida identifies the unknown child: her aunt Lavinia, written out of every record after accusing Edmund and the partner of their associate's death. Lavinia died alone in 1998 — or so the registry claims. POV: Cressida. Beat: the family tree grows a hidden branch, and inheritance becomes curse.

chapters.title: Trial by Memory
chapters.summary: Rosalind reconstructs the original partner's death from fragments and realizes the coroner's verdict was steered — by a young detective whose report reads suspiciously like Rosalind's own early prose. Their mentor, DCI Aldous Wren, signed off on it. POV: Rosalind. Beat: the past indicts the investigator; guilt as motive crystallizes.

chapters.title: Wren's Silence
chapters.summary: Rosalind visits the dying, disgraced Wren, who neither confirms nor denies but recites a line from the confession letters verbatim — before any of them were mailed. He has known the ending for decades. POV: Wren. Beat: horror of complicity; the confession has been sung before.

chapters.title: Third Letter, First Threat
chapters.summary: A third letter arrives naming the date: the will reading. It describes Cressida's death in detail too precise to ignore, and thanks Rosalind for 'finally agreeing to listen.' The killer believes Rosalind is a willing recipient of the archive. POV: Rosalind. Beat: deadline set; protector and target bound together.

chapters.title: Harrowgate's Codicil
chapters.summary: Under pressure, Harrowgate admits the disputed codicil disinherits everyone in favor of a trust administered by — Rosalind. Edmund named them executor weeks before dying, citing 'the only honest officer I ever met.' The killer needed Rosalind inside the estate. POV: Harrowgate. Beat: revelation reframes everything; Rosalind was chosen, not coincidental.

chapters.title: The Ledger in the Walls
chapters.summary: Following Mrs. Pell's hint, Rosalind finds Lavinia's hidden ledger behind the nursery wallpaper: decades of payments, silences bought, and a final entry predicting her own murder — witnessed by initials that match the confession's author. POV: Rosalind. Beat: evidence secured, but the house begins to feel occupied.

chapters.title: Night at Vane House
chapters.summary: Someone ransacks the nursery wall overnight; the ledger is gone, and Mrs. Pell is found unconscious at the foot of the stairs. Cressida refuses to leave. Rosalind realizes the killer is staying inside the house, wearing hospitality as camouflage. POV: Cressida. Beat: fear comes home; sanctuary inverted.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal
chapters.summary: Rosalind stages a fake trial transcript — a mock examination of the confession's claims — and leaks that it will be read aloud at the will ceremony, betting the killer cannot bear an imperfect performance of their own story. Okafor, half-convinced, agrees to look the other way for forty-eight hours. POV: Rosalind. Beat: the hunter sets the stage; agency reclaimed.

chapters.title: The Reading of the Will
chapters.summary: At the ceremony, Rosalind reads the fabricated transcript aloud. The room holds its breath until Tobias erupts — not with guilt but with recognition, completing a phrase only the true author would know, then realizing his error as every face turns. POV: Tobias. Beat: climax ignites; the confession sings on cue.

chapters.title: Confession, Sung
chapters.summary: Cornered, Tobias — Lavinia's son, raised on her unfinished accusation — delivers the true confession: he killed Edmund to stop the estate being dissolved before the truth could surface, and staged the letters to force Rosalind, the last honest officer, to finally read the record aloud. Okafor arrests him as the transcript runs. POV: Rosalind. Beat: catharsis laced with sorrow — justice arrives decades late.

chapters.title: What Rosalind Buried
chapters.summary: In the aftermath, Rosalind confesses their own sin to Cressida: as a junior detective they noticed the anomaly in the partner's case and let Wren talk them out of it. Cressida chooses, deliberately, to inherit the truth rather than the money. POV: Cressida. Beat: reckoning without absolution — inheritance accepted on new terms.

chapters.title: The Bookshop Opens Early
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Rosalind reopens the bookshop with a small shelf devoted to Lavinia's recovered writings, donated by Cressida. A final envelope arrives — blank except for a single line: 'The record is closed.' Rosalind files it, unlocked, in the shop window. POV: Rosalind. Beat: quiet resolution; memory preserved, power surrendered, the door left open.
